sources.title: Royal Palace | Tourism Madrid
sources.excerpt: Home to Spain's kings from Charles III to Alfonso XIII, the palace remains the royal family's official residence.

sources.title: La Almudena Cathedral | Tourism Madrid
sources.excerpt: The cathedral was completed in 1993 and consecrated by Pope John Paul II on 15 June that year.

sources.title: Plaza de la Villa | Tourism Madrid
sources.excerpt: Three streets from the square preserve Madrid's original design; Casa de la Villa formerly housed the City Council.

sources.title: Plaza Mayor | Tourism Madrid
sources.excerpt: The square replaced the Arrabal market and became a stage for festivities, coronations, bullfights and public ceremonies.

sources.title: Puerta del Sol | Turismo Madrid
sources.excerpt: Several historic streets converge at this central meeting place, one of Madrid's best-known public spaces.

sources.title: Cibeles Fountain | Tourism Madrid
sources.excerpt: The fountain has stood in Plaza de Cibeles since 1782, surrounded by four major civic and institutional buildings.

sources.title: Palacio de Cibeles | Turismo Madrid
sources.excerpt: The former communications palace opened in 1909 and has housed Madrid City Hall since 2007.

sources.title: Puerta de Alcalá | Turismo Madrid
sources.excerpt: Charles III commissioned the monumental gate, inaugurated in 1778, to replace an earlier sixteenth-century entrance to Madrid.

facts.value: The present palace occupies the western edge of the historic centre opposite the cathedral.
A Muslim fortress and the later Alcázar preceded the current palace, commissioned after the 1734 fire.
It remains the official royal residence and is used for state ceremonies rather than daily family life.
The stop opens the route with the shift from fortified settlement to the seat of monarchical power.
Its principal façade was redesigned to harmonise with the Royal Palace immediately across Calle Bailén.
Plans began in 1879, changed after Madrid became a bishopric in 1885, and construction concluded in 1993.
The cathedral connects the capital's modern diocese with devotion to Madrid's patron, the Virgin of Almudena.
Its unusually recent completion complicates the expectation that a European capital must have an ancient cathedral.
The Lujanes tower, Casa de Cisneros and Casa de la Villa place fifteenth-, sixteenth- and seventeenth-century civil façades in one view.
The streets of Codo, Cordón and Madrid preserve the primitive layout that made the square a main centre of medieval Madrid.
Casa de la Villa was the seat of Madrid City Council, giving the square a long municipal function.
This compact civil ensemble carries both the medieval-town chapter and the emergence of urban government.
Arcades and uniform façades enclose the former open market space at the heart of Habsburg Madrid.
Philip II planned the remodelling of the Arrabal market after moving the court to Madrid in 1561.
The square hosted markets, festivities, bullfights, coronations and other public ceremonies.
It shows how a commercial edge of the medieval town became the ceremonial plaza of a royal capital.
Historic streets including Mayor, Arenal, Alcalá and Preciados converge in this busy central square.
The square changed repeatedly as Madrid grew from the old town into a national capital.
Puerta del Sol functions as a civic meeting point and the symbolic origin of Spain’s radial roads.
Its everyday crowds and national symbols turn the route from courtly Madrid toward the modern public capital.
The fountain, plaza and surrounding institutions form one visible urban scene at the start of Paseo del Arte.
The fountain has stood here since 1782 and originally supplied water to residents, carriers and cavalry horses.
The former communications headquarters now houses Madrid City Hall, which moved here in 2007.
The scene links Charles III’s urban programme, civic infrastructure and the modern municipal capital without duplicating its members as stops.
The granite neoclassical gate has five openings and different decoration on its former inner and outer faces.
Charles III commissioned it to replace an older entrance; the monumental gate opened in 1778.
It marked the road toward Alcalá de Henares and one of the royal access points into Madrid.
The final stop resolves the arc by showing a former urban boundary absorbed into the expanded modern capital.
